quests.instruction: Which spoken form is typical of American English?
quests.hint: Say it at normal speed. In one version the middle consonant is so light it nearly sounds like a 'd'.
quests.explanation: Between a stressed and an unstressed vowel, American speakers usually produce a quick tap [ɾ] instead of a released /t/. The tap sounds like /d/ to many listeners.
quests.dialectNote: This tap is also heard in Canadian, Australian and Irish English, though the details differ.

quests.instruction: Which version would you expect from a General American speaker?
quests.hint: Listen to what happens between the two syllables.
quests.explanation: The /t/ falls between a vowel and an unstressed syllable, so it is tapped in General American: /ˈmiːɾɪŋ/.
quests.dialectNote: This is why 'meeting' and 'medding'-type words can sound alike in American speech.

quests.instruction: Which version has the American tap?
quests.hint: Compare it with 'wader' in your head. What would a listener actually hear?
quests.explanation: American speakers usually tap the /t/ in waiter, so it sounds like /ˈweɪɾɚ/. Context clears up any ambiguity with 'wader'.
quests.dialectNote: In some American varieties, writer and rider still differ by vowel length.

quests.instruction: Which is a common casual London pronunciation?
quests.hint: The apostrophe stands for a brief closure in the throat instead of a normal 't'.
quests.explanation: In London and many other British varieties, /t/ before a syllabic /l/ is often a glottal stop [ʔ]. It is very common in casual speech.
quests.dialectNote: This glottal stop is a feature of casual British speech and not considered a defect.

quests.instruction: Which form contains a glottal stop?
quests.hint: The stop happens at the boundary between the two halves of the compound.
quests.explanation: Glottal stops replace /t/ before consonants in many British varieties, giving /ˈfʊʔbɔːl/.
quests.dialectNote: The same replacement occurs in words like 'network' and 'that's right'.

quests.instruction: Which phrase shows a glottal stop at the end of the first word?
quests.hint: Watch the end of the first word. A crisp release is absent in one form.
quests.explanation: Word-final /t/ is often a glottal stop before a consonant in many British accents. Many American speakers do this too.
quests.dialectNote: The glottal stop is widespread in English, and not confined to any one region.

quests.instruction: Which casual form is common in American English?
quests.hint: Ask what happens to the sounds between 'n' and the second vowel.
quests.explanation: In casual American speech, /t/ after /n/ before an unstressed vowel is often dropped or reduced, so 'winter' can sound like 'winner'.
quests.dialectNote: Careful speech keeps the /t/, so the reduction depends on style.

quests.instruction: Which version fits casual American speech?
quests.hint: Listen for the middle: one version has a brief pause on the consonant.
quests.explanation: The /t/ in the cluster /nt/ is frequently lost in fast American speech, giving /ˈtwɛni/.
quests.dialectNote: Reduction is more likely in fast speech than in careful speech.

quests.instruction: Which version shows a reduced /nt/ pattern?
quests.hint: Try saying both. The first syllable in one form carries a lighter ending.
quests.explanation: The /nt/ before an unstressed syllable can be simplified to /n/ in casual American English.
quests.dialectNote: Common technology words are great for spotting it in real speech.

quests.instruction: Which version keeps the /j/ glide of Southern British speech?
quests.hint: Pay attention to the sound between the 't' and the vowel.
quests.explanation: Southern British keeps /j/ after /t/: /tjuːn/. General American drops it: /tuːn/.
quests.dialectNote: Some British speakers blend it into /tʃ/, making 'tune' sound like 'chune'.

quests.instruction: Which version matches a British speaker?
quests.hint: Look at the third syllable. It either contains a 'y' glide or it does not.
quests.explanation: The /j/ after /θ/ is retained in many British accents, giving /ɪnˈθjuːziæzəm/. American English typically drops it.
quests.dialectNote: The yod-dropping pattern is wider than after /t/ and /n/.

quests.instruction: Which version is typical of American English?
quests.hint: Two features are at work: one in the first syllable, one in the last.
quests.explanation: General American has an unrounded vowel and no /j/: /ˈkɑːstuːm/. Southern British has /ˈkɒstjuːm/.
quests.dialectNote: Double clues help when one feature is hard to hear.

quests.instruction: Which respelling shows a London-style consonant?
quests.hint: Ask what replaces the 'th' sound at the start.
quests.explanation: Th-fronting replaces /θ/ with /f/ in many London varieties, so thing can sound like 'fing'.
quests.dialectNote: The feature is spreading among younger speakers in England.

quests.instruction: Which version is typical of th-fronting?
quests.hint: The voiced 'th' in the middle of the word is replaced.
quests.explanation: In London-style speech, /ð/ becomes /v/ in the middle of words: 'muvver'.
quests.dialectNote: Th-fronting is a well-documented feature of Cockney and Estuary English.

quests.instruction: Which respelling shows th-fronting?
quests.hint: Only one consonant is changed. Find it.
quests.explanation: The final /θ/ becomes /f/, giving 'something' as 'somefing'.
quests.dialectNote: The change is not applied to every word by every speaker.

quests.instruction: Which is the London h-dropping pattern?
quests.hint: The first consonant is absent in one version.
quests.explanation: H-dropping removes the /h/ at the start of stressed words in many working-class London varieties.
quests.dialectNote: H-dropping is stigmatised in some settings but is natural to speakers who use it.

quests.instruction: Which form shows h-dropping?
quests.hint: Listen to the very first sound of the word.
quests.explanation: In accents with h-dropping, initial /h/ is left out: /ˈapi/.
quests.dialectNote: Not all speakers drop /h/ in every word.

quests.instruction: Which is the reduced form used in connected speech?
quests.hint: Pronouns are normally weak. What happens to the 'h'?
quests.explanation: The /h/ in him is regularly dropped in relaxed speech across many varieties, including standard ones.
quests.dialectNote: Function words are usually weakly stressed and lose sounds first.

quests.instruction: Which respelling shows L-vocalisation?
quests.hint: The dark 'l' turns into a vowel-like glide.
quests.explanation: In London and Australian English, dark /l/ can turn into a /w/-like vowel [ʊ], giving 'miwk'.
quests.dialectNote: The change is more frequent at the ends of syllables.

quests.instruction: Which version has a vocalised /l/?
quests.hint: Notice how the word ends. The tongue tip may not reach the roof of the mouth.
quests.explanation: L-vocalisation turns the syllabic /l/ into a /w/-like sound in many London and Australian speakers.
quests.dialectNote: The written spelling 'ple' hides the sound.

quests.instruction: Which form is characteristic of London?
quests.hint: Compare how the second syllable ends.
quests.explanation: The syllabic /l/ becomes a vowel-like glide in London English.
quests.dialectNote: This shows the same pattern in a different word context.

quests.instruction: Which is the casual 'g-dropping' pronunciation?
quests.hint: Listen to the end of the word.
quests.explanation: In casual speech many speakers pronounce -ing as -in, with a tongue-tip /n/ instead of the velar /ŋ/. It's common in all varieties.
quests.dialectNote: It is not a real dropping of 'g': the sound is a different nasal consonant.

quests.instruction: Which version would you expect from a newsreader speaking carefully?
quests.hint: One ending is made with the back of the tongue, the other with the tongue tip.
quests.explanation: Careful, formal delivery favours the -ing ending with the velar nasal /ŋ/. Casual speech often uses -in' with /n/.
quests.dialectNote: Speakers style-shift between the two endings depending on formality and context.

quests.instruction: Which is the reduced casual form?
quests.hint: The vowel is the same. The nasal at the end differs.
quests.explanation: The casual alternant uses /n/ in place of /ŋ/.
quests.dialectNote: Learners who only know the -ing form may struggle to catch it in speech.

quests.instruction: Which version reflects consonant cluster reduction in casual speech?
quests.hint: One version loses the final stop.
quests.explanation: Final clusters like /nd/ are often reduced in casual speech, especially before a consonant.
quests.dialectNote: This feature occurs in all English varieties.

quests.instruction: Which form would you hear in fast conversation?
quests.hint: The consonant between the two words may weaken.
quests.explanation: The /t/ in 'next' is dropped before /d/ in connected speech.
quests.dialectNote: Word-final /t/ often disappears in clusters.

quests.instruction: Which version reflects careful speech?
quests.hint: The final cluster is complete in one version.
quests.explanation: In careful speech the cluster /skt/ is pronounced fully. In casual speech it is reduced to /st/.
quests.dialectNote: Understanding both forms helps in listening.

quests.instruction: Which is a General American pronunciation?
quests.hint: This word combines the vowel contrast and the tap.
quests.explanation: General American has the unrounded vowel and the tap: /ˈbɑːɾəm/.
quests.dialectNote: The combination of vowel and consonant clues makes the American form quite distinctive.

quests.instruction: Which form shows the reduced /nt/ pattern?
quests.hint: In fast speech, the consonant cluster may be simplified.
quests.explanation: The /t/ after /n/ can be lost in casual American speech: /ˈdɛnɪst/.
quests.dialectNote: The reduction is less likely in careful speech.

quests.instruction: Which respelling shows th-fronting?
quests.hint: The first consonant differs; the vowel does not.
quests.explanation: Th-fronting turns initial /θ/ to /f/ in London-influenced speech.
quests.dialectNote: Together with h-dropping and glottal stops, it forms a recognisable cluster of features.
